heading: Hear their stories
lede: These are the stories Aussie farmers tell about how their own government has treated them. Uninvited visits. Security at elderly farmers' doors. Charges laid and quietly withdrawn. Consultation that counted refusals as agreement. Every story below was told to us on camera. No names are used.

stories.title: He rang triple zero. He was the one arrested.
stories.alt: A farmer stands at an open farm gate at dusk, seen from behind.
stories.body: A farming couple had been clear: the transmission company was not welcome on their land. A worker came onto the property anyway, straight past a biosecurity sign. The farmer rang the police to report the trespass. He was the one who ended up arrested and charged. The family spent months fearing the legal consequences before every charge was withdrawn. They believe they were being made an example of, to warn every other farm on the route.
quotes: I rang the police and long story short, I ended up getting arrested myself.
Probably I think the idea was to break us and what it's actually done is bonded us all together and made us much, much stronger.

stories.title: Security guards at an 80-year-old widow's door
stories.alt: An elderly woman's silhouette in a farmhouse doorway with two large backlit figures outside.
stories.body: A retired farming widow in her eighties, whose land is on the proposed route, answered her front door to a so-called liaison officer flanked by security personnel. She was pressed to sign an access agreement for a small sum, and told that if she didn't sign she might miss out later. She ordered them off her doorstep. Her family lodged a formal complaint. It was never even acknowledged.
quotes: There was a so-called liaison officer, also flanked by security, turned up at her front door.
I just didn't think it was very fair to treat someone like that, especially at that stage of life.

stories.title: A young farmer put on the ground at a 'consultation' meeting
stories.alt: A crowded country hall meeting, figures blurred in motion.
stories.body: At one of the project's public meetings, a young farmer tried to bring in a speaker and a microphone so the room could actually hear the questions being asked. Witnesses describe him being manhandled and jostled until he ended up on the ground. He was no threat to anyone.
quotes: I saw them sort of manhandle one of our young neighbours.
It's not like he was bringing in anything, he was any threat to anyone.

stories.title: Consultation by box-ticking
stories.alt: Hands holding a clipboard of ticked boxes in an empty hall.
stories.body: Farmers who attended the consultation sessions say the process was a sham. Contact lists were assembled largely from people who had declined to be contacted, and those refusals were then counted as consultation. Communities realised the meetings were never about listening.
quotes: Most of those contacts have been the people declining to be contacted, but they've created lists, so that's them box ticking that they've done their consultation.

stories.title: 'Do it our way or we'll bully you into it'
stories.alt: A farmer seen from behind facing a line of transmission towers.
stories.body: A CFA captain whose sisters' farms sit on the route describes families being bullied and railroaded into compliance, targeted and given a hard time the moment they refuse to engage. The mental health toll on those families, he says, is hard to comprehend.
quotes: It's do it our way or we'll bully you into it, and I don't believe that is the right way of an Australian government.
They are just getting bullied and railroaded into it.

stories.title: Farmers gagged from talking to their own neighbours
stories.alt: Two people at opposite ends of a supermarket aisle, turned away from each other.
stories.body: A farmer whose family has worked the same land for more than a century says landholders were gagged from telling their own neighbours what was being signed around them. Deals were done underhand, and communities found out too late. Neighbours who never had a dispute in a hundred years no longer speak, and will change aisles in the supermarket to avoid each other.
quotes: They were gagging farmers not to say what they were doing.
They'll go into the next aisle so they don't have to meet them.

stories.title: When the law said no, they changed the law
stories.alt: A hand on a farm fence wire with a government building rising beyond the paddock.
stories.body: Farming families who have paid their rates and obeyed the law for generations watched the rules rewritten around them, again and again, until the government had the powers it needed to come onto their land. The question they ask is the one every Victorian should ask: if it can be done to them, who's next?
quotes: They keep changing legislation two, three, four times to change the rules to enable them to do anything they want. So if they can do it to us in this instance, what's next? Who's next?

stories.title: A renewable energy zone imposed on a community that said no
stories.alt: A small group of people seen from behind, dwarfed by turbines and transmission towers.
stories.body: A farmer and engineer describes how her community told the government, clearly and repeatedly, that nearly 90% of landowners would not host renewable energy infrastructure. The zone was imposed on them anyway — enforced, in her words, in a vicious and aggressive way, without listening and without care. The community has been left torn apart.
quotes: How would a renewable energy zone where nearly 90% of the landowners are saying that they will not host any renewable energy infrastructure, and why would you impose that on people unless you plan to force this infrastructure onto that land?
It's been torn apart and shattered by this horrific, useless, unnecessary project.

stories.title: Challenged on a neighbour's land — by the people trespassing on it
stories.alt: A line of farmers on a gravel roadside verge, seen from behind.
stories.body: At a peaceful roadside protest to protect a neighbouring property, farmers were asked by project personnel whether they had permission to be on the landowner's property. They did. The people asking didn't.
quotes: Then he asked all us if we had permission to be on her property, which we said, "Well, yes, we do, but you don't."

stories.title: The toll: they go to bed thinking about it
stories.alt: A solitary silhouette at a farmhouse kitchen table before dawn.
stories.body: Behind every incident is what it does to people. Farmers on the route describe the mental anguish of watching their family's land threatened: it is the last thing they think about at night and the first thing in the morning. Some liken the prospect of losing their paddocks to losing a family member. Communities that survived drought, fire and flood together are being broken by their own government.
quotes: You go to bed thinking about it, you wake up in the morning thinking about it.
I've heard people liken it to the loss of a family member.
